# DEV sync

Eric works on a Mac and a Windows laptop. GitHub (`erash11`, all private) is the transport. This skill makes the current machine match GitHub without losing anything on either side. It is the first thing to run when sitting down at a machine.

## Step 0: find DEV (never depend on cwd)

Eric may run this from anywhere. Detect the machine and go to its DEV root:

- macOS (`uname` = Darwin): `~/DEV`
- Windows (PowerShell, or `$OS` = Windows_NT): `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`

If that folder does not exist, stop and say so. Do not guess another location. Print the root you chose on the first line of output.

## Step 1: config and skills

These are separate repos and the other machine may have changed them:

1. `~/.claude` (repo `dotclaude`): `git pull`. If `~/.claude/machine.md` is missing, copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` for this OS.
2. `~/.claude/skills` (repo `claude-skills`): `git pull`, then run `sync-to-codex.sh` (Mac) or `sync-to-codex.ps1` (Windows) so Codex sees the shared skills.
3. `~/.claude/global-memory` (repo `claude-global-memory`): `git pull`. **This is the only thing that carries memory between the two machines.** USER.md, MEMORY.md and the handoffs live here. `daily-backup` pushes this repo nightly, but nothing pulled it at the start of a session until this step existed, so a same-day handoff (worked on the Mac after lunch, picked up on Windows that evening) arrived with stale memory. Pull it before anything else reads it. If the pull brings in commits, say how many and name the newest, so it is visible that memory moved.

If any of the three has local uncommitted changes, commit them first with `<machine> snapshot before sync`, then pull, then push.

4. **Mirror project memory across the two slugs.** Tier A memory is keyed by a slug built from the absolute path, so every project has a Mac folder (`-Users-kristinarash-DEV-X`) and a Windows folder (`C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-X`) under `~/.claude/projects/`. dotclaude carries both to both machines, but each machine auto-loads only its own. Before this step existed, 43 memories written on the Mac never loaded on Windows (found 2026-09-24). After the pulls above, run:

   - Mac: `python3 ~/.claude/skills/dev-sync/mirror_memory.py`
   - Windows: `python $HOME\.claude\skills\dev-sync\mirror_memory.py`

   It copies files one side lacks, lets the newer version win when both have one (frontmatter `modified:`, else last commit), merges `MEMORY.md` indexes line by line, creates the twin folder when a project has memory on only one machine, and never deletes. The older side of any replaced file stays in dotclaude history. Put its summary line in the Step 4 report. If it wrote anything, commit `~/.claude` with `<machine> memory mirror` and push, so the other machine gets the result on its next sync.

   Mirroring is a union: a memory deleted on one machine comes back from the other. To retire a memory for good, delete it from both slug folders in the same commit.

Merge note for `global-memory`: `transcripts/.errors.log` and `MEMORY.md` are both append-heavy and both machines write them. On conflict, keep both sides' content rather than choosing one — these are logs, not settings, and a dropped line is a lost memory.

## Step 2: inventory (always show before changing anything)

Walk `DEV/*`, `DEV/Football/*`, and `DEV/SpecialRequests/*`. Skip `.claude`, `_tools`, `_DRIVE` (a link to the Google Drive primary storage drive, not a project; never init it, never walk into it), `token-dashboard` (someone else's remote), and any folder ending in `_OLD_merged*`. For each folder report one of:

- **repo + erash11 remote**: uncommitted count, unpushed count
- **repo, no remote**: needs `gh repo create`
- **not a repo**: needs init + create (use the `new-project` skill's file set)

Then `gh repo list erash11 --limit 300 --json name` and list repos with no local folder. Skip: `dotclaude` (that is `~/.claude`), `SecondBrain`, `claude-skills`, `claude-memory-compiler`, `DEV`, `DexaProject`.

Eric pre-approves these operations; the inventory is for visibility, not a pause for approval, unless something looks wrong (a repo with hundreds of uncommitted files, a large file about to be added).

**Group the report by activity, not alphabetically.** Run `~/.claude/scripts/dev-activity.sh` (Mac) or `dev-activity.ps1` (Windows), which ranks repos by distinct commit days over 90 days. List the active ones individually and collapse the rest to a count: "118 dormant repos: all clean" is the useful line, not 118 names. About 14 repos are genuinely worked at any time; the rest are archives that happen to live in the same folder.

Rank by **commit days, not recency**. On 2026-09-09 a bulk migration gave 43 repos one commit each, after which every one of them looked active by any recency measure. Days-worked is not fooled by that, because a migration touches a repo once.

Nothing is archived or moved on the strength of this. Sorting is a reporting concern. Moving a dormant repo into an archive folder would break three things at once: `harvest-dev-docs` reads `<dir>/docs/*.md` without recursing, so archived repos would silently drop out of the memsearch index; KeystoneOS `projects.json`, `memory-sources.json`, `memory-index-paths.json` and `discovery-roots.json` hold DEV paths; and Tier A project memory is keyed by a slug derived from the absolute path, so moving a repo orphans its memory. Checked 2026-09-12. Do not revive the archive idea without fixing all three first.

## Step 3: apply, per repo

1. If uncommitted: put any untracked file over 95 MB and any `.env` into `.gitignore`, then `git add -A && git commit -m "<machine> snapshot before sync"`.
2. `git fetch origin` then `git merge --no-edit origin/<branch>`.
3. On conflict: keep this machine's version, save the remote version beside it as `<file>.from-mac` or `<file>.from-windows` (whichever the other machine is), stage both, commit. Never discard either side. `.DS_Store` conflicts: just delete the file.

   Save the remote side by **moving the file, never by redirecting stdout**. A
   redirect re-encodes the bytes; on Windows that silently mangles every
   non-ASCII character (an em-dash becomes `ΓÇö`) and adds a UTF-8 BOM, so the
   saved copy is corrupt and every later diff shows a phantom first-line change.

   - PowerShell: `git checkout --theirs -- <f>; Move-Item <f> <f>.from-mac; git checkout --ours -- <f>`
   - bash: `git checkout --theirs -- <f> && mv <f> <f>.from-mac && git checkout --ours -- <f>`

   Never run `git add -A` while `.git/MERGE_HEAD` exists — it stages the
   conflict markers themselves and commits a broken file. Stage only the named
   paths you just resolved.
4. `git push`.
5. Missing locally: `gh repo clone erash11/<name> DEV/<name>`.
6. No remote: `gh repo create erash11/<name> --private --source=. --push`.

Windows note: line-ending noise (`LF will be replaced by CRLF`) is normal. If a merge refuses to start because of phantom modifications, run `git add --renormalize .` and commit before merging.

Stale-lock note: if a commit or push fails with `cannot lock ref 'HEAD'`, check
`pgrep -fl git` (or `Get-Process git`) first. If no git is running and the
`.git/*.lock` file is zero bytes and older than the session, it is stale from an
interrupted run. Move it aside — do not delete it — then retry.

## Step 4: verify and report

Re-walk every repo. Report: DEV root used, config and skills pulled (yes/no), the memory-mirror summary line, repos checked, pulled, cloned, created, and any folder still dirty or unpushed. List every `.from-*` file created so Eric can reconcile them. Finish with one line: clean or not.

## Step 5: pick up where the other machine left off

Syncing git state is only half the job. The other half is loading the context that came with it, and nothing else does this — the SessionStart hook injects global memory, but project state lives in the repo, and Tier A project memory only crosses machines through the Step 1 mirror. This step is the only place that repo context gets read back in.

Do this for the repo Eric names, or the one he is in. If he has not named one, pick from the ACTIVE list in Step 2, not from all 132: take the active repo with the most recent commit and say which you chose. A dormant repo receiving one migration commit must never win this, which is exactly what picking by recency across everything would do.

1. Read `<repo>/AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md` if there is no AGENTS.md).
2. Read `<repo>/docs/STATUS.md`.
3. Read the newest file in `<repo>/docs/handoffs/`, if the folder exists and its newest file is within about two weeks.
4. If `docs/STATUS.md` does not exist in a repo that has real work in it, say so — that repo is invisible to the other machine and closeout should have created it.

Then report, in six lines or fewer, before doing any work:

```
Picking up: <repo>
Last session: <date>, <mac|windows>
Where things stand: <two lines from STATUS.md Current state>
Blocked on: <open questions, or "nothing">

```

Stop there and wait for Eric to confirm or redirect. Do not start the next task off the back of STATUS.md on your own — it records where work stopped, not what he wants to do this morning.

## Do not

- Do not `rm` anything. Move to a `_to_delete` or `_OLD_*` folder if something must get out of the way.
- Do not rebase or force-push.
- Do not push DexaProject or any repo whose CLAUDE.md says its data must stay local.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security and performance advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations
- SQL runs on the project's database server. Never read server-side files or run OS commands via SQL.

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

# Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive. Every project repo carries a Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` + read `docs/STATUS.md` at start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, `git push` at end.
# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), the expected deliverable is always a produced file. Verify what exists first, then create the artifact regardless — never conclude with "it already exists" instead of delivering the file.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools, not a gate. Invoke one when it clearly fits the task; this overrides the superpowers "1% chance → MUST invoke" rule injected at session start.

# Session Startup

Handled by the `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook — do not read these files by hand. It injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot.

- If `.errors.log` content appears, surface it once on the first response, then continue. It is normally empty; entries mean hook failures.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response instead of working around it.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- What the hook injects is a frozen snapshot. Mid-session writes take effect next session. Never load more than this proactively.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`

entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
